7.1 — Tilemaps: The Level Editor

You are standing in a cave you did not build. The Platformer scene already holds a real cave — a floor, walls, and a way out on the left-hand wall — painted onto a grid before you ever opened the project. And you cannot add a single rock to it, because you have no paint tray and no idea where the art lives. Today you find the art, load the palette, and take ownership of a level that is already half-built. There is no script in this lesson: the editor is where a level actually lives, and today the editor is the work.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I build a level out of tiles?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

You are standing in a cave you did not build, and you cannot add a single rock to it. As one problem that is not startable, because "build a level out of tiles" names nothing you could open: there is no paint tray loaded, no known home for the art, and no way to tell which of the grids under the cave is the one that can stop you.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Find the art the cave was cut from, and load a palettewhat does this part do?Read: the Project window under Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/, the Window ▸ 2D ▸ Tile Palette menu entry, and the window tour in 1.2
  2. Read the Grid, and treat its cell size as a contractwhat does this part do?Read: the Grid component in the Inspector for Platformer ▸ Grid, and the Inspector reading you practised in 1.2
  3. Decide which tilemap you are painting into — solid, exit, or picturewhat does this part do?Read: the three children under Platformer ▸ Grid, and the tag-versus-layer callout in 6.2 where you put the Ground layer on two of them
  4. Paint with the five tools the palette gives youwhat does this part do?Read: the toolbar of the Tile Palette window, and the build-once-stamp-many habit from 2.4
  5. Prove the paint is real — stand on itwhat does this part do?Read: the three components on Platformer ▸ Grid ▸ Collision in the Inspector, and the ground check and its gizmo from 6.2

Notice what the split is doing: only one of those five parts is about making a picture. The other four are about which of three grids you are writing into, how far apart the cells are, and whether the thing you drew can stop you. That is the shape of every level-building problem for the rest of the year — the drawing is the easy half, and what a drawing means to the physics engine is the half that decides whether you have a level or a wallpaper.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Build a level out of tiles" cannot be looked up. "Which window holds the tray of tiles" can — and so can "which component decides whether a painted tile can stop me", because that one has an Inspector page with three names on it.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

The palette holds finished tiles and the tileset folder holds the art they were cut from. Say which one you drag into the tray, and say what a change to the picture would have to travel through to reach every place you have already painted it.

Your grid's cell size is a number somebody chose before you opened the project. Say what would happen to a cave painted at one tile per cell if that number were halved — and say whether the remedy is the grid or the cave.

The Problem: Extending Someone Else's Cave ~10 min

Open Assets/_Scenes/Platformer.unity and press Play. You can walk, you can jump, you stand on rock. Now try to change that rock. Select things in the Hierarchy until you find what the floor is made of. You will land on a Grid with three children under it — and the middle one is the reason this hour is about choosing which tilemap you paint into.

ObjectWhat it is forWhat it already has
Grid The snapping contract. Every child tilemap snaps to its cell size, and every system built on top of the level inherits that spacing. A Cell Size of 1 by 1, and three tilemap children.
Collision (child) The rock you stand on. 75 tiles, filling a box roughly 16 tiles wide and 10 tall — a cave shape, not a solid rectangle. A Tilemap Collider 2D, a Composite Collider 2D, a Rigidbody 2D whose Body Type is Static, and the tag Ground. Physics already works. Leave all of it alone.
Cave Exit (child) The way out. Two tiles, at the far left of the floor — the smallest solid thing in the scene, and the one everybody forgets. The same three components as the floor, and Untagged, because it was built for a different job: SceneSwitch.cs sits on it and sends you to the Overworld when you touch it.
No Collision (child) Pure picture. Backdrop, decoration, anything the player should see but never bump into. It holds 85 tiles — more than the floor does. A Tilemap Renderer, and nothing else. No collider of any kind, so nothing here can ever stop you.

So the level editor already exists and the physics already works. What is missing is everything you need to keep building: the palette — the tray of tiles you paint from — and the location of the art it is made of. Open Window → 2D → Tile Palette. You get an empty window. Now go find the art.

Where the cave art actually lives. Everything this project owns for the cave sits under Assets/Artwork/Platformer/:
  • Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/CavesTileSet/ — the cave, already sliced into individual Tile assets (each one a small .asset file paired with a sprite). 1,829 of them.
  • Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/CaveEntranceTileSet/ — the cave-mouth pieces, sliced the same way. 250 of them.
  • Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/Caves.prefab and CavesEntrance.prefab — these two are Tile Palettes, saved as prefabs. The tiles are already arranged in a grid inside them, and each one carries a Palette Settings component that says so.
  • Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/MainLev2.0.png and Assets/Artwork/Platformer/OriginalFiles/ — the raw source sheets, for when you need to re-slice.
There is no Assets/Sprites folder and no Assets/Tilemaps folder in this project. If you have been told otherwise, that was for a different project.

Socratic: Why a Grid and Not a Pile of Sprites?

  1. Before today every platform in your level was placed by hand — a sprite dragged in and its Transform typed one number at a time. Which two things did you have to do by hand in that world that the Grid now does for you?
  2. A tilemap stores your level as a grid of numbers plus a table of what each number means. What does that buy you that a scene full of loose sprites cannot offer? Think about file size, and think about how a program could read your level.
  3. The scene already has three tilemaps under one Grid, and two of them are solid while the third is only picture. Why would a designer bother splitting one cave into three grids instead of painting everything into one?
  4. The Collision tilemap carries the tag Ground. Tags belong to GameObjects, not to tiles. What does that tell you about how physics and scripting see a whole tilemap — as many objects, or as one?
Read Function-Level Examples ~10 min

A grid of numbers plus a legend is one of computing's oldest ideas. Read each of these for what it does in isolation, then work out what it has to do with a cave. None of these is from a video game.

Example 1 — A subway map's legend, in a route-planning app:

// The map file stores "3" at every station cell.
// Somewhere else, one table says: 3 means "interchange".

Example 2 — A spreadsheet cell reference on a warehouse inventory sheet:

string cell = ColumnLetter(col) + row.ToString();
// R4 is one address. The value at R4 is the whole content.

Example 3 — A printing press's letterpress tray:

// The page is a grid of slots. The tray holds one physical
// block per character, and the press stamps the same block
// wherever the grid asks for it.

Example 4 — A hospital's bed-occupancy board (comment only):

// A ward is a grid. "Occupied" is a value in a cell, not a
// separate object standing in the room.

Example 5 — A theatre's lighting desk (comment only):

// Two grids can cover the same stage: one for the lights that
// cast shadows, one for the lanterns the audience only sees.

Predict Before You Paint

  1. In the subway example, one number means "interchange". In your tilemap, what plays the role of that number, and where is the table that says what it means?
  2. The letterpress tray holds one block per character and stamps it in many places. What is the equivalent of the tray in the Tile Palette window, and what is the equivalent of the page?
  3. Example 5 describes two grids over one stage — one for shadow-casting lights, one for decorative lanterns. The Platformer scene has three over one cave. Which of the three is the shadow-casting grid, and which are the lanterns?
Build Lab: Load the Palette and Extend the Cave ~30 min

Step 1 — open the paint tray. In Window → 2D → Tile Palette, use the palette selector to open the Caves palette that ships in Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/. Tiles should fill the window. If you would rather build your own tray — or the shipped one is arranged confusingly — create a new palette and drag the Tile assets out of Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/CavesTileSet/ into it. Drag the .asset tiles, not the raw PNGs: the slicing is already done for you, and re-slicing a finished sheet is a job you should only take on deliberately. Save a palette you make yourself next to the art it uses, in Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/, so it travels with the project.

Step 2 — choose the right grid. Select Collision in the Hierarchy before you paint rock. Select No Collision before you paint backdrop. Watch the Hierarchy highlight to confirm which one has focus — painting into the wrong tilemap is the single most common first-hour mistake in this unit, and it produces a picture that lies to you.

Step 3 — learn the five tools. The Palette window gives you Paint (drag to draw), Rect (fill a rectangle), Fill (flood a region), Erase, and the Eye Dropper (grab the tile already under your cursor). Paint a 6-tile-wide ledge jutting out of an existing wall, and a two-tile pit floor below it. Then erase half of what you drew and redraw it — the point is the hand, not the level.

Step 4 — paint something and prove it is real. Extend the floor to the right by ten tiles and press Play. Walk onto your new floor. If you can stand on it, you painted on Collision or Cave Exit. If you fall straight through it, you painted on the third grid and now know exactly what "No Collision" means.

There is no code in this lesson, and that is not an oversight. Every build lesson before today ended with a file to type. This one does not, because a tilemap level is editor configuration: a grid, a palette, and a paint stroke. The rung for today is Outline only for exactly that reason — the specification below names the decisions and stops, and the windows are where you make them. Do not go looking for a script to write in this hour.
Architectural specification: before you touch the palette.
  • Which of the three tilemaps must a tile go into for the player to stand on it? Which one is only ever seen?
  • What is the Grid's cell size, and what does every sprite in the cave tileset have in common with that number? (Read the Grid component. Then look at a sprite's Pixels Per Unit in its import settings, if you want the long answer.)
  • If a ledge must be exactly two tiles above a floor so your 6.1 jump clears it, and the grid is 1 unit per cell, how high is that in world units?
  • Where does a palette you build yourself belong, and why there rather than anywhere else in the project?
  • What is the difference between a Tile asset and the sprite it points at? Which one do you drag into a palette, and which one do you edit when you want to change the picture?
  • If you delete a Tile asset that a palette uses, what breaks — the palette, the painted tiles, or both? Predict, then test it on a copy.
The grid is a contract, not a suggestion — and it is already signed. Your collider, your jump arc, your turret placement and your ground check from 6.2 were all tuned against 1 unit per cell. Every tile you paint must land on a cell, and every distance you design must be a whole number of cells. When a layout fights the grid — a gap that wants to be 1.5 tiles — you do not resize the grid. You move the gap. Break that rule and you will spend an evening debugging jumps that are almost possible.
Architectural specification: what you are extending. Read Collision's existing components before you add a tile to it, and answer:
  • What does Tilemap Collider 2D build, and how many of those exist right now for a 75-tile cave?
  • Composite Collider 2D sits beside it on the same object. What is it for, and what happens if you delete it? (You will study this properly in 7.2 — for now, note that it is load-bearing and leave it alone.)
  • The tilemap also carries a Rigidbody 2D. Why would a floor that never moves need a body at all? What Body Type is it set to, and what does the Inspector do to the Gravity Scale field as a result?
  • When you paint one more tile of rock, which of those three components notices, and when — immediately, or on the next Play?
  • There is a third solid object under this Grid that is not tagged Ground. Find it, and say what it is for. Why is it the one a check written against a tag would get wrong?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Say where the cave art lives, and name the two palette prefabs that ship with it
  • Load a palette, and describe the difference between a Tile asset and a sprite
  • Name all three tilemaps under the Grid, say which two are solid and which is only picture, and prove it by painting into each
  • Name all three components already sitting on Collision and what each is for
  • Explain grid-snap as a contract with jumps, colliders and turrets
  • Build the four shapes — step, teeth, shaft, room — and say what each one asks of the player
  • Break this task into parts small enough to look each one up on its own, and say in one line what each part does
  • Say which earlier lesson each part of this task came from, and where you would reread it
  • Commit and push
